headline: Samsung now supplying 1,600-nit VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1400 OLEDs for laptops
summary: Samsung Display is now mass-producing VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1400 OLED panels for laptops, offering up to 1,600 nits peak brightness and improved lifespan.
details: Samsung Display has announced it is now supplying its first mass-produced VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1400 monitor panels to laptop makers. These new tandem OLED displays offer up to 1,600 nits peak brightness, a 40% increase over conventional OLED panels.

The VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1400 certification requires displays to reproduce black levels of 0.0005 nits or lower, while achieving a peak brightness of 1,400 nits at a 10% On Pixel Ratio (OPR). This standard was introduced earlier this month and demands significantly higher brightness than previous tiers.

Tandem OLED display panels utilize an architecture that stacks two organic emissive layers. This design improves light-emitting efficiency, enabling higher brightness and extending the panel's lifespan by reducing the load on each layer.

Laptop brands like Lenovo, Asus, Dell, and MSI are set to integrate these new panels. Lenovo's Yoga Pro 9i Aura Edition was the first device to feature the new tandem OLED, with other devices from Asus, Dell, and MSI expected to launch in the second half of this year.

headline_marked: [[EU is about to sell sensitive data to US]] for visa-free travel, draft agreement suggests
headline: EU is about to sell sensitive data to US for visa-free travel, draft agreement suggests
summary: The draft "Enhanced Border Security Partnership" agreement reportedly allows the US unfettered access to EU citizens' biometric data and other sensitive information. This raises significant concerns about fundamental rights and data protection.
details: The European Commission is reportedly finalizing an "Enhanced Border Security Partnership" (EBSP) Framework Agreement with the US. This deal could allow US border authorities to screen travelers against biometric databases and profile them for security concerns to maintain visa-free travel.

A leaked draft text suggests the Commission has significantly conceded to US demands for broad information access, intensifying travel surveillance and potentially jeopardizing fundamental rights. The US had previously stated that access to biometric databases would be required for countries to retain visa exemption.

While discussions began in 2022, the EU Council officially mandated the Commission to negotiate in December 2025. This Framework Agreement would establish general rules for data exchange, after which individual EU Member States would adopt their own bilateral EBSP agreements with the US.

Critics, including European Digital Rights (EDRi), label the US demands as "blackmail." They express alarm over the systematic transfer of biometric data and subjective "indications of risk" from European databases to the US government.

Concerns are heightened by the US's record on human rights and practices like screening social media profiles, which could lead to discrimination based on political opinions. The sharing of individual risk assessments under the EBSP could target political dissent or support for certain causes.

A May 2026 leak by Statewatch revealed a revised draft, which EDRi's analysis indicates almost entirely reflects US demands. EDRi argues the text deviates from Member States' negotiation mandates and largely fails to comply with EU primary and secondary law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

EDRi warns that the agreement falls short of the EU's fundamental requirement for an essentially equivalent level of data protection for international transfers. They believe the Court of Justice of the EU would likely declare the agreement incompatible with EU law.

EDRi recommends that the Commission and Council resist the US government's pressure and refuse to compromise on personal data. They urge EU leaders to prioritize strengthening core protections against data exploitation and privacy violations.
